input:
Inventory management plays a crucial role in ensuring that production can continue smoothly without unnecessary interruptions, and safety stock is one of the key tools that planners utilise in order to achieve this goal. In the case of the packaging film considered here, demand averages 2399 units per week, although it is important to note that weekly demand is by no means constant, exhibiting a standard deviation of 596 units per week. The replenishment lead time is 4 weeks, which means that, on average, demand over the lead time amounts to 9596 units, while the standard deviation of demand over the lead-time period is 1192 units, reflecting the accumulation of variability across the independent weeks.

Against this background, the safety stock for the packaging film has been set at 1967 units, corresponding to a 95% cycle service level. This means that the policy is designed to provide a high level of protection against stockouts during the replenishment cycle. It should be noted that the underlying calculations rest on certain assumptions, including the assumptions that demand follows a normal distribution and that demand in each week is independent of demand in other weeks. Furthermore, seasonal peaks have been excluded from the analysis, which may potentially affect the adequacy of the 1967 units during peak periods, highlighting the importance of reviewing the policy on an ongoing basis.
target:
Safety stock for the packaging film is 1967 units, held against demand variation over a replenishment lead time of 4 weeks. The cycle service level is 95%: the probability that one replenishment cycle ends without a stockout.

Demand averages 2399 units per week, with a standard deviation of 596 units per week. Mean demand over the lead time is 9596 units, and the standard deviation of demand over the lead time is 1192 units. Weekly demand is treated as independent between weeks, and the lead-time spread follows from that treatment: the standard deviation grows with the square root of the lead time, not in proportion to it, and demand is treated as normal, so the stock is read from the normal distribution at that level.

Two limits stand on the figure. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record, so the 1967 units carry no allowance for them, and a peak that falls inside a replenishment cycle is met from stock sized for ordinary weeks. Independence between weeks is an assumption of the calculation, not a property measured in the record: correlated weekly demand would widen the lead-time spread, and the stock the stated level requires would rise with it.
